title: The stationarity test: a framework for learning quantum many-body systems from their thermal states
abstract: The task of learning the Hamiltonian interactions governing a quantum system, given samples of its thermal (or 'Gibbs') states, is a foundational question at the intersection of quantum learning theory and many-body physics. In this paper, we draw connections to the quantum Gibbs sampling literature to introduce a natural learning algorithm we call the stationarity test: which simply "guesses" the Hamiltonian, and measures the rate-of-change of local observables, under the associated detailed-balanced quantum Markov chain [CKG23]. We leverage the stationarity test to address the following applications:   1. To give the first learning algorithm for the underlying interaction graph, i.e. structure learning, of lattice Hamiltonians at all temperatures, given copies of their Gibbs states.   2. To give the first learning algorithm for the coefficients of a lattice Hamiltonian, given only copies of its thermal metastable states, modeled as the "local minima" of the free energy.   3. In addition, we present a refinement to the recent area law for thermal metastable states [BCV25], which holds in the thermodynamic limit.   Our learning algorithms are rigorous, time-efficient, and nearly sample-optimal in system size and accuracy. At a technical level, our arguments are based on new approximate locality and convexity properties for the quantum Fisher information of these Gibbs sampling algorithms.
summary: This paper introduces the 'stationarity test,' a novel theoretical framework to reconstruct the Hamiltonian of a quantum many-body system using only samples of its thermal Gibbs states. It provides rigorous algorithms for both determining the interaction structure and estimating the coupling coefficients. By connecting this test to the Quantum Fisher Information, it offers a powerful tool for quantum machine learning in condensed matter physics.
main_problem: The core problem is learning the unknown Hamiltonian interactions governing a quantum many-body system solely from samples of its thermal (Gibbs) states.
main_result: The authors introduce the 'stationarity test' as a rigorous framework to perform structure and parameter learning for lattice Hamiltonians, even when only metastable states are accessible.
method: The method centers on the stationarity test, which measures the rate-of-change of local observables under the dynamics generated by a guessed Hamiltonian, linking this test to the Quantum Fisher Information.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum many-body systems modeled by lattice Hamiltonians, $H = \sum h_\gamma P_\gamma$, whose thermal equilibrium states are the Gibbs states, $ho_H = e^{- eta H} / 	ext{tr}[e^{- eta H}]$.
key_observables: Local observables ($O$), the rate-of-change measured by the stationarity test ($	ext{Test}_i$), and the Quantum Fisher Information (FIG).
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), system size ($n$), approximation error ($\eta$), and the locality/distance parameter ($\ell$).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that the stationarity test yielding zero implies the guessed Hamiltonian is close to the true one, and it extends to using metastable states instead of true Gibbs states.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the stationarity test framework, details algorithms for structure learning from Gibbs states, and presents extensions for parameter learning using thermal metastable states, concluding with a refinement of the area law for these metastable states.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, data-driven theoretical tool to characterize the underlying physics (Hamiltonian) of complex quantum systems using only measurements of their thermal equilibrium or near-equilibrium states, which is highly relevant for simulating and understanding open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A cartoon of the “neighborhood guessing” structure learning algorithm. A ground truth 2- local Hamiltonian H lies on the edges of an unknown square lattice. The current guess Hamiltonian G (edges in blue) is a strict subgraph of H (missing edges in dashed black). In each iterative step, we “guess” the neighborhood of a qubit, by perturbing G+U with a small cluster U of 2-local terms (orange). The stationarity test then evaluates the rate of change of 2-local observables (purple), evolved under LG+U, truncated to a finite radius (gray) around the origin.

Figure 2: A cartoon of the Hamiltonian learning problem from metastable states. A metastable state (orange gradient) lies in a double well, depicting a toy model of the free energy landscape of low temperature, 2D Ising model configurations of average magnetization x (black curve). The learning algorithm guesses a Hamiltonian, and attempts to “fit” to the free-energy landscape (blue curve), by checking if the sampled state is also metastable w.r.t. the guess. See Question 1.9.

Figure 3: The sample-optimal neighborhood guessing algorithm. (a) The Test associated to a locally perturbed Hamiltonian G+ηU is computed by first estimating the test under the current Hamiltonian G, truncated to radius R ∼log η−1 (gray). This ‘baseline’ is refined by local measurements at radius L (red) around the perturbation (17). (b) The sites are partitioned into disjoint ‘colors’ (only 3 pictured), each with non-overlapping radius R balls, and performed in parallel. A randomization scheme is used to address observables (purple) crossing balls of the same color (see Algorithm 4).
